title: clustOpt: Quickstart Guide
text: clust_opt() function calculates several metrics beyond silhouette scores help evaluate clustering quality. Let’s examine full output:

title: clustOpt: Quickstart Guide
text: metric provides different perspective clustering quality: avg_width: Average silhouette score across test cells. Measures well-separated clusters (range: -1 +1, higher better). cluster_median_widths: Median silhouette score per cluster, averaged. KLdivergence: Kullback-Leibler divergence D_KL(training || predicted). Measures much predicted cluster proportions test subject differ training data. Lower values indicate reproducible clustering (0 = identical distributions). Hellinger: Hellinger distance training predicted cluster proportions. Similar KL divergence symmetric bounded (0 1). Lower better. modularity: Measures clustering quality using k-nearest neighbor graph (k=20). Higher values indicate cells cluster assigned neighbors rather cells clusters (range: -0.5 1, higher better).

title: clustOpt: Quickstart Guide
text: metrics assess whether cluster proportions reproducible across subjects. subject held : Random Forest predicts cluster assignments test subject predicted cluster proportions compared training cluster proportions Lower values indicate different subjects produce similar cluster compositions resolution. important reproducible resolution identify underlying cell populations regardless subjects used training. KL Divergence asymmetric can approach infinity cluster present training completely absent predictions Hellinger Distance symmetric bounded (0-1), providing stable comparison metrics use pseudocount 1 handle clusters may missing predictions.
code: cv_results |>   drop_na() |>   ggplot(aes(x = as.factor(resolution), y = KLdivergence)) +   geom_boxplot() +   theme_bw() +   labs(     title = "KL Divergence by Resolution",     x = "Resolution",     y = "KL Divergence"   ) cv_results |>   drop_na() |>   ggplot(aes(x = as.factor(resolution), y = Hellinger)) +   geom_boxplot() +   theme_bw() +   labs(     title = "Hellinger Distance by Resolution",     x = "Resolution",     y = "Hellinger Distance"   )

title: clustOpt: Quickstart Guide
text: Modularity measures whether predicted cluster assignments partition data’s neighborhood graph better expected chance: k-nearest neighbor graph (k=20) constructed test data projected onto clustering PCs Modularity compares fraction edges within clusters expected edges distributed randomly (preserving node degrees) Modularity complements silhouette scores capturing local connectivity patterns rather global distances.
code: cv_results |>   drop_na() |>   ggplot(aes(x = as.factor(resolution), y = modularity)) +   geom_boxplot() +   theme_bw() +   labs(     title = "Modularity by Resolution",     x = "Resolution",     y = "Modularity"   )

title: clustOpt: Quickstart Guide
text: selecting optimal resolution, consider guidelines: Silhouette scores: Look resolutions scores high stable across subjects. Declining silhouette higher resolutions often indicates -clustering. KL Divergence / Hellinger: Lower values indicate reproducible cluster proportions across subjects. Increasing values higher resolutions suggest clustering becomes subject-specific rather capturing shared biology. Modularity: Higher values indicate predicted clusters match local neighborhood structure test data. Decreasing modularity higher resolutions suggests clusters becoming subject-specific don’t generalize well. encourage look plots metrics picking resolution. suggest_resolution() function uses rank aggregation approach help pick resolution performs well across metrics conflict:

title: calculate_hellinger_distance — calculate_hellinger_distance
text: Calculate Hellinger distance two probability distributions. Hellinger distance symmetric measure bounded 0 1, 0 indicates identical distributions 1 indicates distributions overlap.

title: calculate_hellinger_distance — calculate_hellinger_distance
code: calculate_hellinger_distance(q, p)

title: calculate_hellinger_distance — calculate_hellinger_distance
text: q Numeric vector representing first probability distribution. Must non-negative sum 1. p Numeric vector representing second probability distribution. Must non-negative, sum 1, length q.

title: calculate_hellinger_distance — calculate_hellinger_distance
text: Numeric value 0 1 representing Hellinger distance.

title: calculate_hellinger_distance — calculate_hellinger_distance
text: Hellinger distance calculated : H(P, Q) = sqrt(0.5 * sum((sqrt(p) - sqrt(q))^2)) Unlike KL divergence, Hellinger distance symmetric: H(P, Q) = H(Q, P).

title: calculate_hellinger_distance — calculate_hellinger_distance
code: # Identical distributions p <- c(0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25) calculate_hellinger_distance(p, p)  # Returns 0 #> [1] 0  # Completely different distributions (no overlap) q <- c(1, 0, 0, 0) p <- c(0, 1, 0, 0) calculate_hellinger_distance(q, p)  # Returns 1 #> [1] 1

title: calculate_kl_divergence — calculate_kl_divergence
text: Calculate Kullback-Leibler divergence two probability distributions. D_KL(Q || P) measures much information lost P used approximate Q. result always non-negative, 0 indicating identical distributions.

title: calculate_kl_divergence — calculate_kl_divergence
code: calculate_kl_divergence(q, p)

title: calculate_kl_divergence — calculate_kl_divergence
text: q Numeric vector representing "true" probability distribution. Must non-negative sum 1. p Numeric vector representing "approximating" probability distribution. Must non-negative, sum 1, length q.

title: calculate_kl_divergence — calculate_kl_divergence
text: Numeric value representing D_KL(Q || P), always >= 0.   Returns 0 distributions identical.

title: calculate_kl_divergence — calculate_kl_divergence
text: KL divergence calculated : D_KL(Q || P) = sum(q * log(q / p)) Note KL divergence asymmetric: D_KL(Q || P) != D_KL(P || Q). q[] > 0 p[] = 0, divergence infinite. implementation requires elements p positive corresponding elements q positive.

title: calculate_kl_divergence — calculate_kl_divergence
code: # Identical distributions p <- c(0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25) calculate_kl_divergence(p, p)  # Returns 0 #> [1] 0  # Different distributions q <- c(0.5, 0.3, 0.1, 0.1) p <- c(0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25) calculate_kl_divergence(q, p)  # Returns positive value #> [1] 0.2180119
